claims.text: A computational approach integrating machine learning with ab initio phonon calculations will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional models.
The target materials are homogenized, disordered high-entropy-alloy solid solutions intended for thermal-insulation applications.
The proposed framework combines data-driven algorithms with ab initio phonon calculations to estimate thermal conductivity.
The approach is applicable when composition is well defined and the alloy remains a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution within a stable temperature regime.
Atomic-scale disorder in high-entropy alloys produces mass fluctuations.
Atomic-scale disorder in high-entropy alloys produces force-constant fluctuations.
Mass and force-constant fluctuations enhance phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Learning from ab initio-calculated phonon spectra allows the method to incorporate local compositional fluctuations and force-constant variations.
Representing local compositional and force-constant variations enables more accurate modeling of phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering lowers phonon thermal conductivity.
The integrated approach will reduce prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional models based on average properties.
The integrated approach will reliably identify alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity arising from enhanced phonon scattering.
Current conventional prediction methods use simplified Debye approximations or average atomic properties without detailed phonon-dispersion analysis.
Phase segregation can limit the applicability of a method that assumes a homogeneous disordered solid solution.
Significant lattice strain can limit the applicability of the proposed method.
Extreme compositions can limit the applicability of the proposed method.
Time-domain thermoreflectance can be used to obtain experimental phonon thermal-conductivity values for the benchmark alloys.
Failure to achieve the expected 20–30% error reduction against conventional models would falsify the claimed accuracy improvement.
Systematic misprediction of alloys experimentally confirmed to be homogeneous would falsify the hypothesis.
